CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the G20 90-day window to negotiate in earnest without adding new tariffs, entity-list style measures, or further detainee actions. Keep the Meng/Huawei file diplomatically live and demand her release, but do not collapse the trade channel over it — we have already answered the arrest with the Kovrig/Spavor detentions. Offer to discuss agricultural and energy purchases as a bargaining chip against a permanent freeze of the January List-3 hike, while refusing structural dismantling of industrial policy or Made-in-China 2025.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. Combined US Section 301 coverage is ~$250B (List 1–2 at 25%, List 3 at 10% from 24 Sep), and the same-day-as-G20 arrest of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou is firm-level targeting of a national champion, following the April ZTE denial-order near-shutdown. That maps to the CHN +0.5 anchor (export hit + FX pressure + Huawei targeting + export-hub unemployment risk). Macro already shows strain: China SA merchandise exports fell from $206.3B (Jul) to $196.9B (Dec, −4.5%); imports collapsed −14.9% over the same window; CNY weakened from 6.54 (25 Jun) to 6.89 (19 Dec), having touched ~6.97 in late October; reserves slipped ~1.4% to $3.09T. Contemporaneous reporting (NYT 14 Dec; official Q3 GDP 6.5%) documents factory hour-cuts and early migrant returns in Dongguan/Guangzhou. Offsetting that, the 1 Dec truce suspended the 1 Jan List-3 jump to 25%, industrial production is still expanding (~5.7% y/y), and the US is itself risk-off (VIX 25.6 on 19 Dec). Escalation now would likely invite the postponed 25% hike and a possible remaining-import tranche we cannot fully match. Concession (purchase packages or tariff rollback) is premature: talks are days old, the May 19 “significantly increase purchases” statement was walked back by Washington on 29 May, and one-sided rollback would validate coercion. Negotiate/hold is therefore the action that matches a +0.48 threat: buy time, test whether Washington will trade a tariff freeze for limited commercial commitments, and keep tech-autonomy options open if the 90-day clock fails.
key_factors: G20 90-day truce and suspended 1 Jan 2019 List-3 hike to 25%
Meng Wanzhou arrest on 1 Dec plus ZTE denial-order precedent — Huawei as national-champion risk
US Section 301 already covering ~$250B of Chinese exports at 10–25%
China export/import softening, CNY ~5% weaker vs USD, modest reserve drain
Domestic slowdown (Q3 GDP 6.5%, factory hour-cuts in export hubs) raises cost of further escalation
Canada detentions already taken; further non-tariff retaliation would likely blow up talks
May 19 purchase-truce collapse shows US can reverse verbal deals — do not pre-concede

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended. Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
China detains Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor (widely viewed as retaliation for the Meng arrest; Beijing denies linkage).
List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
China SA merchandise exports: $206.3B (Jul) to $196.9B (Dec), change −4.5%.
China SA merchandise imports: $184.9B (Jul) to $157.3B (Dec), change −14.9%.
CNY/USD 6.536 (25 Jun) to 6.8918 (19 Dec), +5.4% yuan depreciation vs USD over the window.
US VIX 25.58 on 19 Dec, +47.6% over the lookback — US risk-off backdrop during the truce.
China’s economy slows sharply: weak retail sales and industrial production; factories cutting hours; migrant workers sent home early in Dongguan/Guangzhou.
Meng arrest opens a new front; China’s Commerce Ministry still confident a deal can be reached inside the 90-day deadline; Foreign Ministry demands her release.
Both sides have reason to keep talks going; arrest makes domestic politics of a deal harder for Xi; ZTE case was not a one-off.
